title: Transient and busy period analysis of the GI/G/1 queue: The method of stages
contribution: Closed-form Laplace transforms of the transient queue-length and FCFS waiting-time distributions (system initially empty) and of the busy period of MGE_L/MGE_M/1 queues by the method of stages, inverted numerically.
problem_entry: {SD} Transient and busy-period analysis was long held to be very difficult, yet needed for start-ups, new controls and slow convergence (manufacturing, airport runways); exact results existed only for M/M/1, so the field had turned to numerics (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Approximate general distributions by dense MGE stages; solve the Markov chain's homogeneous part by separation of variables with tensor algebra and its boundary/initial part by a closed-form M x M linear system; get the busy period from a queue build-up time matrix whose eigenvalues are given by the same M roots (pp. 2-3, 5-6, 11-16).
assumptions: MGE arrivals and service, FCFS, rho < 1; system initially empty (explicit algebra otherwise very hard, p. 5); distinct roots as a convenience (p. 9); Assumption 1 (stationary arrival phase) for the waiting time, needed only for closed forms (pp. 18, 21).
proof_devices: separation of variables with tensor algebra for the homogeneous Kolmogorov equations (pp. 5-7)
det(I + B) = 1 + trace(B) for rank-one B in the characteristic polynomial (p. 8)
Rouché's theorem for the number of roots (p. 9)
Vandermonde system solved by Cramer's rule (pp. 11-12)
normalization (generating function at z = 1 equals 1/s) and root-symmetry checks (p. 13)
rank-one inverse update and spectral decomposition for the busy period (pp. 15-16)
the s -> 0 limit recovers the steady-state Lindley solution (p. 24)
experiments: Mathematica on a Macintosh II; inversion by Platzman-Ammons-Bartholdi and by Hosono; validated only against exact M/M/1 values for rho from 0.1 to 0.99 (Table 1 at rho = 0.75: Hosono exact, PAB deviates); MGE3/MGE2/1 illustration; largest run MGE20/MGE20/1; no timings (pp. 24-31).
positioning: Set against the numerical tradition (Grassmann's randomization, integration of the Kolmogorov equations); simplifies Ramaswami's matrix-geometric busy period; builds on Bertsimas 1990 (MGE) and Keilson-Zachmann (pp. 2, 5, 13).
writing: A strategy paragraph precedes Theorem 1 (p. 6); a remark says which assumptions are conveniences (p. 9); the introduction promises concluding remarks that the file does not contain (p. 3 vs pp. 24-32).
limits_future: Empty initial state, distinct roots, Assumption 1 and benchmarks only for M/M/1 (pp. 5, 9, 18, 25); next step: a sequel posing GI/G/1 as a Hilbert problem (p. 2).

method_links.note: The representation (MGE stages) is chosen so that a known machinery, Markov chains plus transforms, applies exactly, and the paper says where explicit tractability ends (the initial condition). But the class kept is analytic, not LP, conic or MIO, and no optimization appears: the probability side of Tension T3.
Weak: the lack of benchmarks beyond M/M/1 is stated in the body.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: dense tractable class as the universality device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: MGE stages are dense in all distributions, so exact analysis for MGE is presented as general; the same device appears in S336

transferable: To analyse a queue with general distributions exactly, approximate them by a dense phase class whose stages have a probabilistic meaning (MGE), exploit the Markov structure, and state the price: the number of stages (pp. 2-3).
Split the Kolmogorov equations into a homogeneous part, solved by a geometric (separation-of-variables) ansatz, and a boundary/initial compensation part, solved as a small linear system (pp. 5-6).
Check closed forms by a normalization identity (generating function at z = 1 equals 1/s) and by recovering the known steady-state limit (pp. 13, 24).
Validate a numerical inversion on the one exactly solvable case across the whole load range before illustrating new cases (pp. 25-26).
coauthors: Daisuke Nakazato (MIT ORC; his PhD student, 1990, per 04-mentorship.md)

quotes.text: Transient and busy period analysis in queueing models have long been considered as very difficult problems.
Unfortunately, we did not have any other numerical results to compare with except the ones for the M/M/1 queue

title: On central limit theorems in geometrical probability
contribution: Central limit theorems with convergence rates for the lengths of the kth-nearest-neighbour graph, the Voronoi diagram and the Delaunay triangulation of Poisson points, by conditioning on a high-probability event that makes dependence local.
problem_entry: {SD; combinatorial-optimization graphs as objects} BHH and Steele proved laws of large numbers for TSP, MST and matching on random points; CLTs were believed because dependence 'seems to be local' but were unproved; the entry makes this precise for three computational-geometry graphs, the Delaunay one containing the MST (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Find an event A_n with P(A_n) -> 1 under which the configuration is m-dependent across O(n/log n) subcubes holding 1 to O(log n) points each, then apply Baldi-Rinott's dependency-graph CLT, which also yields rates; this replaces Bickel-Breiman's long fourth-moment proof (pp. 2-5).
assumptions: Poisson process of intensity n on [0,1]^2, points in general position with probability 1 (pp. 2-3); subdivision m = floor((n/(c log n))^(1/2)) with c > 5/4 (p. 5); the uniform i.i.d. model is not covered (p. 13).
proof_devices: high-probability good event that localizes dependence (Lemma 2, p. 6)
fixed dependence radius by geometric arguments: R = 4 for the nearest-neighbour graph, R = 6 for Voronoi and Delaunay (Proposition 3, pp. 6-7)
variance lower bound by planting positive-probability local configurations and conditioning (Proposition 5, pp. 8-10)
Baldi-Rinott dependency-graph normal approximation, unconditioned via P(A_n) -> 1 (Theorem 6, pp. 10-11)
rates for the convex-hull CLTs of Groeneboom and Hsing by the same device (Remark 2, pp. 11-12)
positioning: Continues the BHH and Steele laws of large numbers; replaces Bickel-Breiman's fourth-moment proof by a conditioning argument; inspired by Ramey's unsuccessful MST thesis attempt (pp. 1-4).
writing: Turns a folklore belief into a precise event; an 'Intuitive idea' subsection precedes the proofs (p. 4); remarks discuss whether the rates are optimal and state a conjecture (p. 11).
limits_future: For the MST the event is known but its probability cannot be shown to tend to 1; for TSP and matching no such event has been found (pp. 4-5); log factors probably artefacts (p. 11); future: d dimensions and the uniform Euclidean model (p. 13).

method_links.note: Only step 5 (print the boundary) is present: the paper states exactly where its device stops (MST, TSP, matching; Poisson model only). There is no formulation in a solver class: the probability side of Tension T3.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: condition on a high-probability event that makes dependence local, then apply a dependency-graph CLT with rates
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Subcube occupancy event, fixed dependence radius, Baldi-Rinott bound; the same device gives rates for known convex-hull CLTs

transferable: To prove a CLT for a sum whose dependence is local, find a high-probability event under which dependence has a fixed finite range; condition on it, apply Baldi-Rinott, and remove the conditioning with P(A_n) -> 1; the rate then picks up the failure probability (pp. 4-6, 10-11).
Lower-bound a variance by planting many disjoint positive-probability local configurations and using Var >= E[Var | F] (pp. 8-10).
Choose the subdivision scale just large enough for the good event (lambda about c log n), and say which part of the rate comes from that choice (p. 11).

quotes.text: we succeeded in proving CLTs for the length of three graphs
In contrast, for the MST we know the event, but we cannot show its probability tends to 1.

title: Decomposition algorithms for analyzing transient phenomena in multi-class queuing networks in air transportation
contribution: Two decomposition algorithms that extend an exact single-airport transient recursion to airline networks by feeding delays forward into downstream schedules, tested against simulation and used for hub-connectivity and slack policy questions (read in the Operations Research 1995 version).
problem_entry: {SD + AP} Hub-and-spoke banks propagate delay between airports; the single-airport model ignored airport interaction, and transient network analysis existed only as diffusion approximations or special cases; the intended use is strategic planning of connectivity and slack, set against an airline's historical-data simulation (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Run the single-airport moment recursion at each node, period by period, and update downstream arrivals: Algorithm 1 by expected waits net of slack, Algorithm 2 by two-moment waiting-time densities, per-aircraft delay probabilities and Bernoulli-sum arrival counts (pp. 4-9).
assumptions: Landing runways as one server; deterministic time-varying demand; Markov capacity states (semi-Markov allowed); slack per itinerary leg (pp. 2-4); for tractability: updates by expected values, independent contributions, normal arrival counts, network collapsed to its hubs (pp. 6, 8-9).
proof_devices: moment recursions with complexity O(S^2 K^2 Qmax) per airport (p. 3)
complexity of Algorithms 1 and 2, O(N S^2 K^3 Qmax) and O(R N S^2 K^3 Qmax) (pp. 5, 9)
restart every m periods: 3,240 to 360 iterations at K = 80, m = 10 (p. 5)
two-moment fit of an atom-plus-exponential waiting-time law, with an exponential fallback (pp. 6-7)
experiments: Two-hub network, test cases of Table I (case 1 DFW-like); benchmark is a reduced-form simulation with 10,000 replications propagating realized delays (C, Ultrix DECsystem 5900); agreement in case 1, 0-30% discrepancy in case 2 (deviations 6.11 and 5.69) and similar in case 3; about 10 and 30 min against 5 min for the simulation (pp. 9-13).
positioning: Extends the authors' 1992 single-airport model; similar in spirit to Whitt's QNA; contrasted with diffusion approximations and with American Airlines' simulation built on historical flight times (pp. 1-2).
writing: The abstract states the negative accuracy result; the conclusion gives four numbered findings and argues for analytical over empirical models (pp. 1, 15).
limits_future: Delay propagation underestimated in heavy traffic, results partly discouraging (pp. 1, 13); future: capture tail delays without enumerating sample paths (p. 15).

method_links.note: Application-led model with DFW-like data and policy what-ifs (connectivity, slack), but the benchmark is the authors' own simulation rather than the owner's current rule, and there is no field test.
Two operational knobs (connectivity p, slack) with their trade-offs read off (hub isolation protects other hubs but worsens the isolated one), but no bound and no price curve.
A student paper with the co-adviser (Peterson with Odoni, per 04-mentorship.md), part of a thesis turned into two journal papers (S135, S659).
The negative accuracy result is printed in the abstract and in Section 4.2.

transferable: Decompose a transient network: run the exact single-node recursion node by node and period by period, passing delay information downstream; benchmark against a simulation that differs only in the approximation under test (realized vs expected updates), so that the gap isolates that approximation (pp. 4, 11-13).
When only two moments are available, fit a mixed atom-plus-exponential distribution suggested by simulated histograms, with a fallback when the moment condition fails (pp. 6-7).
When a recursion restarts every period, restart it only every m periods (m = minimum time between an aircraft's stops) and report the iterations saved (p. 5).
Collapse a large network to the nodes whose delays matter (the hubs) and treat the others as fixed (p. 9).
coauthors: Michael D. Peterson (PhD 1992, co-advised with Odoni per 04-mentorship.md), Amedeo R. Odoni (his own PhD adviser)

quotes.text: Thus, the results are at least partly discouraging for the approximation procedures.
Case 1 suggests that for networks of airports like DFW, waiting times are probably not high enough to create significant network effects on a frequent basis

title: Models and algorithms for transient queueing congestion at airports
contribution: A transient landing-queue model with deterministic time-varying demand and Markov or semi-Markov weather-driven capacity, solved by an efficient moment recursion and applied to Dallas-Fort Worth data for schedule-interference and demand-smoothing questions.
problem_entry: {SD + AP} Hub-airport delays (banks of up to 40 flights in 30 minutes); steady-state, phase-type and diffusion approaches do not fit time-varying demand, weather-dependent capacity and dependent service times; the aim is a planning tool for a proposed daily schedule (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Treat demand as deterministic per 15-minute interval and capacity as a Markov or semi-Markov weather process, so each interval is a fluid step and queue and waiting-time moments follow from a backward recursion over (period, capacity state, age, queue length) (pp. 3-5).
assumptions: Known arrivals per interval (Assumption 1) and S capacity states with arbitrary discrete holding times (Assumption 2); deterministic service within an interval, no aircraft-type separations, strategic not operational (pp. 3-4); data: DFW March 1989 schedule, EPS capacities corrected by UNISYS, capacity history rebuilt from 8 years of NOAA weather (pp. 7-8).
proof_devices: semi-Markov process recast as Markov on an age-augmented state (p. 4)
Theorems 1-3 and Corollary 4: recursions for first and second moments, the waiting time at the boundary split into in-interval and later parts (pp. 4-5)
Theorem 5: memory O(SKMQmax), time O(S^2 K^2 M Qmax), factor M dropped in the Markov case (p. 6)
experiments: chi-square tests reject geometric holding times but occupancies match and Markov and semi-Markov outputs coincide (5 min vs about 2 h on a DEC-3100); deterministic vs time-varying Poisson arrivals over 10,000 simulated days; DOT on-time validation, predicted queueing delay about half of total lateness (250 vs 540 min) with matching peaks; policy runs on start state, i.i.d. capacity, bank interference and smoothing (pp. 8-16).
positioning: Builds on Odoni-Roth and Green-Kolesar's case against steady-state approximations; contrasts phase-type Kolmogorov solutions (including Bertsimas-Nakazato), diffusion approximations, and the airport studies of Newell, Koopman, Abundo and St. George (p. 2).
writing: Opens with press figures and delay statistics (p. 1); states validation caveats bluntly (pp. 11-12); closes with policy insights rather than theorems (p. 16).
limits_future: Validation data unfit for the purpose (pp. 11-12); service dependence not modelled (p. 4); upstream delays deferred to the network follow-up (p. 7); smoothing beyond a level creates costly excess capacity (p. 16).

method_links.note: Real data from the airport authority, DOT, OAG and NOAA; the status-quo schedule is the baseline; policies are scored in decision units (minutes of delay, share of flights displaced); evaluation limits stated. No field test (step 6 missing).

One knob (the arrival cap L per 15 minutes), a priced curve (average delay 6.05 -> 3.29 -> 2.43 min against 7.23% and 17.37% of flights moved) with a knee, handed to policy makers; computed by the model, no solution-independent bound.

The model class is chosen by measured run time: semi-Markov dropped for Markov after the outputs prove insensitive, in the spirit of the stop rule's measured solve time; the class is a recursion, not LP or MIO.
A student paper with the co-adviser (Peterson with Odoni, per 04-mentorship.md).
The rejected chi-square tests and the weak DOT validation are printed in the body.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: choose the model class by measured run time after showing the decision outputs are insensitive
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: semi-Markov vs Markov capacity: fit rejected, outputs equal, 2 h vs 5 min, so the Markov model is adopted; S659 keeps the Markov formulation for the same reason

transferable: When one model feature is expensive (semi-Markov holding times), test its fit (chi-square), then test whether the decision outputs change; if not, adopt the cheaper model and report both run times (pp. 8-10).

Before validating against imperfect field data, say what the data measure and what they do not; trim outliers by a stated rule; report the aggregate gap (250 vs 540 min) and what matches (peak timing) (pp. 11-12).
Price a policy knob with a two-column table, benefit (average delay) against cost (share of flights moved), at two settings, and read off the knee (Table 4, p. 16).
When the uncertainty process is persistent, report results conditional on the starting state: averaging hides a factor of about 3 (pp. 12-13).
coauthors: Michael D. Peterson (PhD 1992, co-advised with Odoni per 04-mentorship.md), Amedeo R. Odoni

quotes.text: On balance, Figure 6 is of limited usefulness.
smoothing policies exhibit diminishing returns and increasing costs.

title: Branching bandits and Klimov's problem: Achievable region and side constraints
contribution: Exact polyhedral achievable region for average-cost branching bandits and Klimov's problem with general distributions, a lifted description with O(R^2) variables and constraints, and a polynomial-time algorithm giving side-constrained optimal policies that randomize among at most L + 1 priority rules.
problem_entry: {SD + LO (+IO)} Klimov's problem and branching bandits with linear side constraints such as fairness; earlier polyhedral characterizations had exponentially many constraints, and side-constraint results gave structure but no usable algorithm for several constraints (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Characterize the achievable region of mean-queue-length vectors as a polyhedron whose extreme points are priority policies, so that control becomes LP; give a lifted polynomial-size polyhedron whose projection is exactly that region; decompose LP optima into at most L + 1 extreme points (pp. 1-2, 5-8, 10-11).
assumptions: Nonpreemptive service, arbitrary independent service and offspring distributions; Assumption A: spectral radius of E[N] below 1 and exponential-type tails, the latter much stronger than needed and relaxed at the end (pp. 2-3, 11-12); M/GI/1 is the most general Klimov setting (G/GI/1 counterexample, p. 3).
proof_devices: square the one-step evolution equation and take stationary expectations to get conservation inequalities (Theorem 3.2, p. 5)
extreme points = priority policies by adjacency plus a perturbation argument (pp. 5-6)
auxiliary second-moment variables I_ji = E[x_j N_i] giving an O(R^2) lifted description (Theorem 4.1, pp. 7-8)
Palm-to-stationary passage for time averages (Lemma 5.1, pp. 8-9)
Caratheodory plus a basic optimal solution: at most L + 1 priority rules (pp. 6, 10)
convex decomposition by an exit-point LP and LP sensitivity analysis to find a facet, recursing over R stages (pp. 10-11)
positioning: Philosophically different from bandit-index approaches (Gittins, Weiss); refines the exponential characterizations of Tsoucas and Bertsimas-Nino-Mora; extends the potential-function method of the authors and Kumar-Kumar from exponential to general distributions; judges Nain-Ross and Makowski-Shwartz algorithmically unusable for several constraints (pp. 1-2).
writing: States the philosophical contrast in the introduction (p. 1), lists three numbered technical contributions (p. 2), and concedes that the decomposition step is much harder than it looks (p. 2).
limits_future: Open: networks with general distributions; whether every extended polymatroid is a projection of a polynomial-size polyhedron; the lift has extreme points no policy attains (pp. 11-12).

method_links.note: Owning tradition and tool named (bandit indices); variables are performance vectors; the class is kept (LP, also with side constraints) and made polynomial by a lifted formulation; boundary printed (G/GI/1 counterexample, networks open, unattainable extreme points of the lift).
A co-advised student paper with Tsitsiklis (Paschalidis, per 04-mentorship.md) in the achievable-region lineage.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: lift-and-project to a polynomial-size extended formulation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Exponentially many conservation inequalities replaced by O(R^2) lifted equalities whose projection is exactly the achievable region; extended polymatroids posed as a general question
Klimov's problem becomes a special case of branching bandits; exponential characterizations recovered; potential-function method extended to general distributions

transferable: To get linear constraints on a stochastic system's performance vector, square the one-step evolution equation and take stationary expectations; each subset-priority rule makes one inequality tight (p. 5).
Lift with auxiliary second-moment variables (I_ji = E[x_j N_i]) to replace exponentially many constraints by O(R^2), then check whether the lift's extreme points are achievable (pp. 7-8, 12).

To realize an LP optimum as a policy, decompose it into at most L + 1 extreme points (Caratheodory plus a basic optimal solution), read them as priority rules and randomize among them per busy period (pp. 6, 10).
Relax a technical tail assumption by approximating with exponential-type variables of the same means and variances when the constraints depend only on those moments (pp. 11-12).
coauthors: Ioannis Ch. Paschalidis (student, co-advised with Tsitsiklis per 04-mentorship.md), John N. Tsitsiklis

quotes.text: We are thus able to convert a difficult stochastic control problem to one of optimizing a linear cost function over the achievable region, and this is a linear programming problem.
as it turns out, this is much more complicated than it might have appeared at first sight.

title: Stability conditions for multiclass fluid queueing networks
contribution: An LP test, built from a decomposition of fluid trajectories, that is necessary and sufficient for stability of all work-conserving policies in two-station multiclass fluid networks and is shown by LP duality to be equivalent to piecewise linear Lyapunov functions; sufficient conditions for more stations.
problem_entry: {SD + LO} Networks with feedback can be unstable under priority and FIFO policies although every load is below one; the exact stability region was open, and it was unknown whether convex Lyapunov functions can certify it exactly (p. 1).
key_idea: Decompose every feasible two-station trajectory into four phase types and sum time and work per phase into LP variables; LP[Q(0)] bounds the strong busy period, and stability holds if and only if LP[0] has only the zero solution (pp. 2-7).
assumptions: Fluid model (alpha, mu, P, C) with substochastic routing of spectral radius below 1; work-conserving policies; stability as emptying in finite time; load condition rho < e assumed (p. 2).
proof_devices: trajectory decomposition into phase types (Proposition 1, pp. 2-3)
LP bound on the strong busy period, and a lower bound by minimizing (Proposition 2, pp. 3-5)
sufficiency via boundedness of LP[Q(0)] when LP[0] admits only zero (Theorem 1, p. 5)
necessity by constructing a periodic work-conserving trajectory from a nonzero LP solution (Theorem 2, pp. 6-7)
LP duality: the dual of Down-Meyn's Lyapunov LP is a relaxation of LP[0], equivalence via Lemmas 5-7 (pp. 8-12)
positioning: Sharper than the Lyapunov-function sufficient conditions of Kumar-Meyn, Botvich-Zamyatin, Dai-Weiss and Down-Meyn; relies on Dai's fluid-limit theorem; shows Down-Meyn's LP is exact for two stations (pp. 1, 7-8).
writing: Numbered contributions mapped to sections, with an explicit admission that necessity for more stations could not be proved (p. 1).
limits_future: Exact only for two stations; the conditions for more stations are conjectured necessary; transfer to stochastic networks only suspected (p. 1); the J-station theorem is on file page 13, which has no text; an authors' correction (1997) is recorded in 04-mentorship.md (not read); the author biography lists the Erlang Prize 1996 and the SIAM Best Publication Award in Optimization 1996, without naming works (p. 14).

method_links.note: Owning tradition (Lyapunov stability analysis) and its tool named; variables over a describable set (time and work per trajectory phase); stability becomes an LP test; dualization reads the rival certificate as the dual relaxation (step 4); boundary printed (more than two stations: sufficient only).
A co-advised student paper with Tsitsiklis (Gamarnik, per 04-mentorship.md).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: trajectory decomposition into phase-type LP variables, with a periodic-trajectory construction for necessity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Time and work per phase type become LP variables; only-zero LP[0] certifies stability; a nonzero solution yields an explicit unstable periodic policy

transferable: Turn stability under every policy into an LP: classify states by which resources are busy, sum time and work per phase type over a whole trajectory and write conservation per phase; only the zero solution then certifies stability (pp. 2-5).
Prove necessity by converting a nonzero LP solution into an explicit adversarial, periodic policy (pp. 6-7).
When a rival method certifies by an LP (here the Lyapunov LP), take its dual and compare it with your own LP to settle exactness (p. 8).
Use the homogeneous LP (zero right-hand side) for qualitative questions and the inhomogeneous one for quantitative bounds, here upper and lower bounds on the busy period (pp. 3-5).
coauthors: David Gamarnik (student, co-advised with Tsitsiklis per 04-mentorship.md), John N. Tsitsiklis

quotes.text: Using linear programming duality, we show that for two-station systems the Lyapunov function approach is equivalent to ours and therefore characterizes stability exactly.
although we were unable to establish necessity.

title: A unified method to analyze overtake free queueing systems
contribution: Shows that the distributional laws are special cases of H = lambda G and turns them into a unified asymptotic (heavy-traffic, arbitrary renewal arrivals) and exact (MGE arrivals) method for the distributions of L, Q, S and W in overtake-free queues, with new results for GI/G/1, GI/G/infinity, vacations and priority queues.
problem_entry: {SD} Asks for the laws of queueing theory by analogy with Maxwell's equations: the field solves applications case by case; Little's law lacks second-moment information, so H = lambda G is the candidate (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Derive the Haji-Newell distributional law from H = lambda G, apply it to both queue and system in overtake-free systems, and solve a 4 x 4 system of transform relations (L-S, Q-W, S = W + X, L-Q) for all four distributions (pp. 2-5, 12, 15).
assumptions: Single arrivals and departures, FIFO exit, no effect of later arrivals on earlier customers (Assumptions A, p. 4); overtake-free means A holds for queue and system (p. 8); heavy traffic needs L, Q, S, W -> infinity (pp. 9, 11); MGE (or PH) arrivals for exact results (p. 15); an independence approximation for GI/G/infinity (p. 14).
proof_devices: indicator-process construction to derive the distributional law from H = lambda G (pp. 4-5)
Smith's asymptotic method for renewal kernels: Taylor expansion in s, partial fractions, expansion around z = 1 (Theorem 3, pp. 9-10)
asymptotic PASTA through the arrival coefficient of variation (p. 11)
six-step asymptotic and exact methods as solved transform systems (pp. 12, 15)
eigen-decomposition of A0 + zA1 and analyticity to get the MGE/G/1 waiting time without Hilbert factorization (Theorem 7, pp. 16-18)
positioning: Builds on H = lambda G (Whitt, Miyazawa, Heyman-Sobel), Haji-Newell, Keilson-Servi and Bertsimas-Nakazato; generalizes the P-K formula, PASTA, the Fuhrmann-Cooper decomposition and the results of Doshi and Lucantoni et al. (pp. 2-3, 18-19).
writing: Opens with a Maxwell's-equations analogy and a rhetorical question (pp. 1-2); presents each method as a numbered six-step procedure (pp. 12, 15).
limits_future: Overtake-free systems are a small subset of applications; laws for systems with overtaking (GI/G/s, networks) are the open problem (pp. 33-34).

method_links.note: The formulation-first instinct in probabilistic form: find the right set of laws so one method solves a class, and say where the class ends. No optimization: the probability side of Tension T3.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: P-K formula, PASTA, Fuhrmann-Cooper and Keilson-Servi results recovered as special cases, then generalized

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: dense tractable class as the universality device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: MGE called the simplest class of distributions dense in the space of all distributions; the same device as S220

transferable: Derive a distributional law from H = lambda G by choosing an indicator process h(t) and per-customer quantities g_j so that both sides become probabilities of the event of interest (pp. 4-5).

Write a method as a fixed sequence of transform relations (the customers-time law for system and queue, S = W + X, a system-specific L-Q link), solve the resulting 4 x 4 system, and reuse it across models (pp. 12, 15).
For heavy traffic, expand the renewal kernel around s -> 0 and z -> 1, keep the leading exponential, and check that the answer becomes exact in the Poisson case (pp. 9-13).
coauthors: Georgia Mourtzinou (MIT ORC; his PhD student, 1995, per 04-mentorship.md)

quotes.text: What are the laws of queueing theory?
The major open problem is to identify queueing laws for systems that allow overtaking, which lead to a complete solution.

title: Improved randomized approximation algorithms for lot-sizing problems
contribution: Randomized-rounding proofs of the 94% and 98% power-of-two bounds for nested lot sizing that do not depend on the optimal solution's structure, a unification of both bounds, and improved 1.043 (fixed base period) and 96.9% (one-warehouse multi-retailer, O(n)) guarantees from stronger relaxations.
problem_entry: {IO, operations-management application} Multi-product nested lot sizing under power-of-two policies; the incumbent is Roundy's tight deterministic rounding (98% and 94%), reused across extensions; the entry is to re-derive and improve those bounds by randomized rounding (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Round each relaxed order interval up or down by one shared random threshold whose distribution equalizes the expected setup and holding ratios; derandomize over the breakpoints (recovering Roundy); strengthen the relaxation by piecewise linearization over {T_L, 2T_L, 3T_L} and mix 2^p and 3*2^p grids (pp. 4-10).
assumptions: Constant demand, infinite production rate, echelon holding and ordering costs, stationary nested policies (p. 1); convex relaxation solvable in polynomial time, O(n log n) on trees and O(n) on stars (p. 2).
proof_devices: expected-ratio computation E[T^R]/T and T*E[1/T^R] under a designed rounding distribution (Theorems 1-2, pp. 4-6)
derandomization by sorting fractional parts: at most n + 1 outcomes (pp. 5-6)
Lemma 5: optimal relaxed values below 3T_L lie in {T_L, 2T_L, 3T_L} (p. 8)
mixture of two rounding grids with case analysis (Theorem 6, pp. 9-10)
six case relaxations for the OWMR problem, each O(n) (Lemmas 8-10, Theorem 11, pp. 11-13)
positioning: Recasts the deterministic rounding of Roundy and Maxwell-Muckstadt as randomized rounding in the Raghavan-Thompson, Goemans-Williamson and Bertsimas-Vohra tradition; Roundy's 98% algorithm recovered by derandomization; extensions match Federgruen-Zheng (pp. 2-3, 6, 13).
writing: Bullet contributions with percentage effectiveness (94%, 98%, 97%, 96.9%) as the headline unit (pp. 2-3, 7, 13); no abstract and no concluding section in the file.
limits_future: No limits or open questions stated (no concluding section); extensions claimed almost for free because the proofs do not use the structure of the optimal solution (pp. 3, 13).

method_links.note: Formulation first in the IO sense: a convex relaxation, strengthened exactly where rounding loses (piecewise linearization; six case relaxations); but the deliverable is a rounding guarantee, not a model kept in a solver class. Also evidence for the strong-formulation side of Tension T4.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: designed-distribution randomized rounding, derandomized by breakpoint enumeration, recovering the incumbent's deterministic rule
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Rounding distribution chosen to equalize the K/T and HT ratios; derandomization over n + 1 breakpoints gives Roundy's 98% algorithm
94% and 98% bounds as endpoints of one family of base-period choices (p = 2 already 97%); Roundy's algorithm as a derandomization

transferable: For a cost K/T + HT, choose the rounding distribution so that the two expected ratios E[T^R]/T and T*E[1/T^R] are equal, then maximize over the fractional position; one shared random threshold preserves monotone constraints T_i >= T_j (pp. 4-5).
Derandomize a threshold rounding by sorting the fractional parts: only n + 1 distinct outcomes, so try them all (p. 5).

Strengthen the relaxation where the guarantee is lost: linearize the objective over the few discrete values small variables can take, and mix two rounding grids (2^p, 3*2^p) with tuned probabilities (pp. 7-9).
Split the problem into a few cases (T_0 >= 6T_L or T_0 = kT_L), solve a stronger relaxation for each, and take the best (pp. 11-13).
coauthors: Chung-Piaw Teo (MIT Sloan and ORC; his PhD student, 1996, per 04-mentorship.md)

quotes.text: Our proof is simple and unlike the original deterministic rounding does not depend on the structure of the optimal solution.
Roundy's 98% algorithm can be obtained by derandomizing our algorithm.
